items.prompt: A database has multiple copies, but a user can still lose a committed transaction when the Region fails. What distinction should the architect make?
constraints: The business has a data-loss objective.
Replication behavior is not yet verified.

options.text: Durability of stored copies and availability of the service are related but distinct; measure replication lag and recovery point against the RPO.
Any replica guarantees zero data loss and zero downtime.
Availability replaces the need to define data durability.
More copies automatically make every write synchronous.

feedback.Reason: Multiple copies do not by themselves define when data is durable or whether the service remains available.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Durability concerns preservation of data; availability concerns successful access; replication mode and lag determine recovery freshness.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team identifies acknowledged-write semantics, measures lag, and tests restore or failover against the RPO and RTO.
Details.errorCorrection: Replicas can be asynchronous, availability does not guarantee data preservation, and copy count does not change write semantics.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Synchronous coordination can reduce data loss but may increase latency and failure coupling.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Replication has explicit semantics and may not be synchronous.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A service can be available while losing unreplicated recent data.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Copy count does not establish synchronous acknowledgement.

items.prompt: An operator accidentally deletes an object and needs to recover the prior version. Which S3 control helps?

options.text: Enable versioning, protect or govern deletion as appropriate, and test restoring a prior object version.
Enable default encryption only; encryption keeps deleted versions automatically.
Use a shorter lifecycle expiration so recovery happens faster.
Disable object ownership controls.

feedback.Reason: S3 Versioning preserves distinct object versions and supports recovery from accidental overwrites or deletes.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A delete marker or new version can leave prior content available until lifecycle or governance removes it.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner tests version retrieval and delete permissions and aligns lifecycle retention with the recovery requirement.
Details.errorCorrection: Encryption protects content but does not retain deleted versions, short expiration harms recovery, and ownership controls do not provide version history.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Version retention consumes storage and needs lifecycle and deletion governance.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Encryption does not create object history.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Ownership settings address access and control, not version preservation.

items.prompt: A cross-Region replica is configured, but no one has measured its lag during peak writes. What evidence is missing?

options.text: Measure replication lag and recoverable data age under representative and peak load, then test failover or restore from the replica.
Assume the replica is current because its status is healthy.
Measure only the number of replica instances.
Stop monitoring lag so replication is not interrupted.

feedback.Reason: A healthy replication status does not prove that lag remains within the RPO under the workload's peak behavior.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Replication lag and recoverable point age are workload-dependent and must be measured under the conditions the recovery plan claims to support.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team tests source load, lag alarms, restore output, and traffic recovery from the target Region.
Details.errorCorrection: Status and replica count are indirect, and removing lag monitoring hides RPO risk.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Peak testing consumes resources and may require throttled or isolated traffic, but unmeasured lag invalidates the claim.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A healthy state does not quantify data freshness.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Count does not show whether writes are caught up.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Monitoring is needed to protect the recovery point.

items.prompt: A restore completes without error, but the team has not checked record counts, checksums, or application invariants. What is the risk?
constraints: Restore success is an infrastructure signal.

options.text: The restore may be technically complete but logically unusable; validate integrity, completeness, relationships, and representative application reads and writes.
A successful restore API call proves every record is correct.
Skip validation to avoid changing recovered data.
Validate only the newest object timestamp.

feedback.Reason: Recovery correctness includes data and application validation beyond the storage service's successful operation.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Checksums, counts, relationships, and business invariants detect incomplete, stale, or inconsistent recovery output.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team restores into an isolated environment and runs read-only or safe validation before traffic cutover.
Details.errorCorrection: An API success status is not logical correctness, avoiding all validation leaves defects hidden, and a timestamp is insufficient.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Validation takes time and requires safe test design, but unvalidated recovery can corrupt user outcomes.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Infrastructure success does not prove application-level integrity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Safe validation can be read-only or isolated and is necessary.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: One timestamp cannot establish completeness or relationships.

items.prompt: Where should a backup restore test run when the production database must remain unaffected?
constraints: The backup can be restored to another account or Region.

options.text: Restore into an isolated test environment with controlled access and representative validation, then record the measured recovery result.
Restore over production so the test is realistic.
Test only the backup listing API.
Never test restores because they consume storage.

feedback.Reason: Isolation protects production while allowing the organization to prove that the copy can be restored and used.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A separate account, VPC, or Region can provide blast-radius control while preserving realistic restore and validation steps.
Details.scenarioApplication: Operators restore with least privilege, run integrity and application checks, and clean up according to retention policy.
Details.errorCorrection: Overwriting production is unsafe, an API listing does not prove restore, and never testing leaves the recovery claim unverified.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Isolated tests cost resources and need data protection controls, but they are essential evidence.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A restore-over-production test creates unacceptable blast radius.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Metadata presence does not prove recoverability.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Storage cost is not a reason to abandon recovery evidence.

items.prompt: An operator needs to recover a database to just before an accidental deletion. Which capability is most relevant?
constraints: The target time is within the retention window.
The restore should not overwrite production initially.

options.text: Restore a point-in-time copy to a separate instance, validate it, and decide how to reconcile or promote the recovered data.
Restore only the latest snapshot because it is always closest to the incident.
Change the database DNS name without restoring data.
Delete the current database so the service recreates the previous state.

feedback.Reason: Point-in-time recovery selects a recoverable time rather than limiting the operator to the latest snapshot.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Continuous logs or recovery records allow a new database instance to be created at a selected time within retention.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team restores separately, verifies the data, and plans cutover or reconciliation without destroying the current evidence.
Details.errorCorrection: Latest snapshot may include the deletion, DNS does not recreate data, and deletion is destructive.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Point-in-time recovery has retention, restore-time, and storage considerations and still requires validation.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: The latest snapshot can contain the accidental deletion.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Naming does not restore database content.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Deleting the current copy removes evidence and does not restore a chosen time.

items.prompt: A DynamoDB table must recover from accidental writes without losing the current production table. Which approach fits?
constraints: The target time is in retention.

options.text: Restore the table to a new table at the chosen time, validate items and indexes, then plan a controlled application cutover.
Delete the table and recreate it from an empty template.
Use a CloudWatch alarm to reverse every write automatically.
Restore over the production table without checking access or data.

feedback.Reason: Restoring to a new table preserves production evidence and allows correctness validation before cutover.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: DynamoDB point-in-time restore creates a new table from a selected recovery point and requires application-level transition planning.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner checks item counts, indexes, permissions, streams, and consumers before switching traffic.
Details.errorCorrection: Deletion loses data, alarms cannot reverse arbitrary writes, and unvalidated replacement can break access or semantics.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Restore and migration take time and can require dual-read or dual-write coordination.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: An empty template does not recover data.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Monitoring cannot reverse arbitrary database writes.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Direct overwrite removes a safe validation boundary.

items.prompt: A regulated workload must retain backups for a defined period and prevent routine operators from deleting them early. Which design is appropriate?
constraints: Retention is a business and compliance requirement.

options.text: Use a governed backup vault or retention control with least-privilege deletion, documented retention, and periodic restore tests.
Allow every administrator to delete backups to simplify operations.
Keep retention only in a spreadsheet.
Use the shortest retention because compliance data is rarely restored.

feedback.Reason: Retention and deletion governance protect the recovery history while restore testing proves it remains useful.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Backup controls can restrict deletion and enforce lifecycle behavior independently of ordinary workload administration.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner configures retention, separates recovery permissions, and tests restore without weakening the retained copy.
Details.errorCorrection: Broad deletion defeats governance, a spreadsheet is not enforcement, and low restore frequency does not reduce retention obligation.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Governed retention can increase storage cost and requires an exception process.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Broad deletion access defeats the recovery control.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Low restore frequency does not justify violating retention.

items.prompt: A critical application has not had a restore test in 18 months despite multiple schema and IAM changes. What should the owner do?
constraints: The RTO and RPO remain approved.
Production must be protected during testing.

options.text: Run a controlled restore and recovery exercise now, compare results with objectives, and trigger tests after material changes as well as on a defined cadence.
Keep the annual cadence because recovery tests are unrelated to application changes.
Test only the backup job status.
Wait for a real outage to validate the new schema.

feedback.Reason: Recovery tests must reflect current dependencies, permissions, schemas, and artifacts, not a historical design.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Change-driven and periodic testing exposes drift before an incident and protects recovery claims.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team restores in isolation, exercises current workflows, and updates the runbook and objective evidence.
Details.errorCorrection: Application changes can break recovery, job status is not restore proof, and a real outage is an unsafe test.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Tests consume time and resources, so their scope should align with criticality and change risk.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Material changes invalidate a fixed test assumption.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A successful backup job does not test restore or application use.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: An outage is too late to discover recovery drift.

items.prompt: A cross-Region replication stream stops, but the destination remains reachable. Which alert is most important for the recovery objective?
constraints: The recovery point depends on replication.

options.text: Alert on replication failure or lag beyond the RPO and link it to a runbook that restores the replication path or declares reduced recovery readiness.
Alert only when the destination Region is unreachable.
Ignore replication because old backups exist somewhere.
Alert on destination CPU only.

feedback.Reason: A reachable destination with stale data can still violate recovery readiness.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Replication status and lag directly measure freshness and determine whether the target meets the RPO.
Details.scenarioApplication: Operators repair or replace the replication path and record the interval of degraded recovery protection.
Details.errorCorrection: Network reachability and CPU do not show data freshness, and older backups may not meet the same RPO.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Alert thresholds need noise control while still preserving enough response time before the recovery point expires.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A reachable Region can still have stale data.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Older backups may not satisfy the current objective.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: CPU is not a replication freshness signal.

items.prompt: Which failure test best validates a Region recovery plan for an application with replicated data and Route 53 failover?
constraints: The application has a safe test path.

options.text: Isolate or withdraw the primary path, execute the documented failover, measure data point, traffic transition, user success, and rollback, then restore normal service.
Stop one web process in the primary Availability Zone only.
Check the Route 53 record without withdrawing any dependency.
Compare resource counts between Regions.

feedback.Reason: A regional recovery claim needs a controlled test of the regional failure boundary and the complete user path.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Failure injection validates detection, routing, data freshness, capacity, application behavior, and restoration rather than one component.
Details.scenarioApplication: The exercise has a blast-radius guard, a timed runbook, user validation, and a rollback or return-to-primary step.
Details.errorCorrection: One AZ process failure is narrower, record inspection does not test routing behavior, and resource counts do not prove service recovery.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Regional tests require careful scheduling and safeguards but provide stronger evidence than component checks.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: An AZ process failure does not exercise the Region path.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A record check without failure does not validate failover.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Counts do not measure user behavior or data point.

items.prompt: A restore test fails because the recovery role lacks permission to create the target database and read the backup. What should be changed?
constraints: The permissions must be tested before an incident.

options.text: Grant the documented minimum recovery permissions to the dedicated role, validate them in a test, and monitor their use.
Give every operator administrator access permanently.
Skip permissions testing and grant access during the outage.
Make the backup public so any role can read it.

feedback.Reason: Recovery authorization is a prerequisite and should be least-privilege, explicit, and exercised before an incident.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A dedicated recovery role and policy must cover backup read, target creation, key use, networking, and validation actions.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team runs a preflight or restore test with the role and alerts on unexpected permission or usage changes.
Details.errorCorrection: Permanent admin access violates least privilege, incident-time grants delay RTO, and public backups violate protection.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Recovery roles need enough authority for an emergency but should be bounded by account, Region, resource, and approval controls.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Broad permanent admin access increases compromise and error risk.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Missing permissions discovered during an outage extend recovery.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Public backup access is an unacceptable data-protection failure.

items.prompt: A team wants to restore production customer data into a shared developer account for recovery testing. What is the safer choice?
constraints: The restore test must not expose production data.

options.text: Use an isolated controlled account and appropriately mask or minimize sensitive data while preserving the behaviors needed for the recovery test.
Copy the full production dataset because testing needs exact values.
Make the restored bucket public temporarily.
Skip recovery testing for sensitive systems.

feedback.Reason: Recovery evidence must protect data while still testing the critical structure and behavior.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Isolation, least privilege, and masking or minimization reduce exposure in nonproduction recovery tests.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner defines representative test data, restricts access, logs use, and validates recovery workflows without copying unnecessary sensitive values.
Details.errorCorrection: Exact production values increase exposure, public access is unsafe, and sensitive workloads still need a protected recovery test.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Masking can hide edge cases, so test data must preserve relevant distributions and integrity rules.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Exact values are not required for every recovery test and increase exposure.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Public access creates an unacceptable data breach risk.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Sensitive data requires stronger test controls, not no evidence.

items.prompt: A restore test finishes in 25 minutes, but the report measures only database creation and not application startup or traffic return. Can it claim a 30-minute RTO?
constraints: The RTO is end to end.

options.text: No; repeat the test from the declared incident start through usable application traffic and record every critical-path milestone.
Yes, because database creation is always the longest step.
Yes, if the backup is encrypted.
No test can measure RTO because outages are unpredictable.

feedback.Reason: The unmeasured steps can exceed the remaining five-minute budget and invalidate the RTO claim.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: RTO ends when the service is usable and validated, not when one infrastructure action completes.
Details.scenarioApplication: The report includes restore, bootstrap, dependencies, routing, user tests, and recovery operator actions.
Details.errorCorrection: Longest-step assumptions are unverified, encryption does not establish timing, and controlled exercises can measure recovery.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Repeated tests need a safe schedule and consistent start and end definitions.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Unmeasured application and traffic steps may be longer.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Encryption is unrelated to end-to-end timing proof.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Uncertainty is why controlled recovery tests are needed.

items.prompt: A backup depends on a chain of incremental backups, and one link is missing. What should the recovery owner verify?
constraints: The backup product has a dependency chain.
Recovery must be possible from a selected point.

options.text: Verify chain completeness and perform a restore from the intended point instead of assuming the latest catalog entry is sufficient.
Delete the latest backup so the service falls back automatically to a valid copy.
Check only the backup file size.
Increase retention without repairing or testing the chain.

feedback.Reason: A cataloged backup may depend on prior recovery data and must be restored from a complete valid chain.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Backup integrity includes metadata, dependencies, retention, encryption, and the ability to reconstruct a usable point.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team identifies a recovery point, validates chain health, restores in isolation, and alerts on missing links.
Details.errorCorrection: Deletion is destructive, file size is not recoverability, and retention does not repair a broken chain.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Chain validation and restore tests consume time but protect against false recovery confidence.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Deleting evidence cannot create a valid chain.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Size does not prove dependency completeness or logical integrity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: More retention does not repair missing backup dependencies.

items.prompt: A replicated event store can receive writes in different orders after network partition. Which recovery test is essential?
constraints: The system can reconnect after partition.
Duplicate and out-of-order delivery are possible.

options.text: Inject partition and reconnection, then verify ordering, idempotency, reconciliation, and customer-visible outcomes before accepting the replication design.
Check only that both stores contain the same number of records.
Disable retries so no duplicate can ever occur.
Assume network recovery restores event order automatically.

feedback.Reason: Record counts can match while order, duplicates, and business state are wrong after a partition.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Distributed replication needs explicit event identity, ordering or commutativity, replay, and reconciliation behavior.
Details.scenarioApplication: The exercise partitions the paths, reconnects them, replays events, and checks resulting business invariants.
Details.errorCorrection: Counts do not prove sequence, disabling retries loses recoverable work, and transport recovery does not guarantee application order.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Strong ordering can reduce availability or increase coordination latency, so the business semantics must decide.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Equal counts can hide order and content errors.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Disabling retries does not solve partition loss safely.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Network reconnection does not define event ordering.

items.prompt: What evidence best supports a claim that a recovery exercise met the RTO and RPO?
constraints: Both time and data freshness matter.

options.text: Timestamped incident, restore, dependency, validation, and traffic milestones plus measured recoverable data age and the final user outcome.
A screenshot of the recovery dashboard after the exercise.
The number of operators assigned to the runbook.
A statement that no error was reported by the backup service.

feedback.Reason: RTO and RPO claims need direct evidence of elapsed recovery and data freshness tied to a usable service.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Timed milestones and recovery-point measurements make the result auditable and comparable across exercises.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner stores the run log, test data validation, user SLI, failures, and remediation actions.
Details.errorCorrection: A dashboard screenshot and staffing count are indirect, and backup status omits end-to-end recovery.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Evidence collection must protect sensitive data and preserve enough detail for review.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A screenshot lacks timing, data point, and acceptance context.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Staffing does not prove the result.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Backup success is not end-to-end recovery evidence.

items.prompt: A recovery exercise meets the RTO but reveals a data reconciliation defect. How should the result be recorded?
constraints: The exercise outcome must be honest.

options.text: Record the RTO result and the separate correctness failure, block full readiness approval, assign remediation, and retest the complete recovery path.
Declare success because elapsed time is the only recovery metric.
Hide the defect from the recovery report until it is fixed.
Increase backup frequency without understanding the reconciliation defect.

feedback.Reason: A fast but incorrect recovery does not provide a usable service and must not be labeled fully ready.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Recovery acceptance includes availability, data integrity, and business correctness in addition to timing.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner tracks the defect, limits traffic or uses a safe degraded mode, fixes reconciliation, and repeats the test.
Details.errorCorrection: RTO alone is insufficient, hiding evidence creates stale risk, and backup cadence may not address application conflict logic.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Remediation can delay certification, but honest evidence prevents a false recovery claim.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A service with inconsistent data is not fully usable.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: More frequent copies do not automatically fix reconciliation semantics.
